Definition

GERD is a GI disorder characterized by regurgitation of acidic stomach contents into the esophagus or beyond into the mouth, larynx or lungs; leading to irritation and inflammation in these areas

It is the most commonly diagnosed GI disorder in the US, affecting 20% of population

BruceBlaus, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Causes

There is no specific cause for GERD but there is risk factors, those include:

  • Esophageal problem: Esophageal dysmotility => impaired esophageal acid clearance
  • LES problem: Impairment in the tone of lower esophageal sphincter (LES)
  • LES problem: Transient LES relaxation
  • Stomach problem: Delayed gastric emptying
  • Anatomical problem: presence of hiatal hernia
  • Increased intra abdominal pressure in obesity and pregnancy
  • Psychosocial stress
  • Impaired saliva production: saliva neutralize acid
Olek Remesz (wiki-pl: Orem, commons: Orem), CC BY-SA 2.5 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.5>, via Wikimedia Commons

Other risk factors

Age > 50 years

Low socioeconomic status

Tobacco use

Consumption of alcohol

Connective tissue disorders

Postprandial supination

Use of medications including anticholinergic drugs, benzodiazepines, NSAIDs or aspirin, nitroglycerin, albuterol, CCB, antidepressants and glucagon

Clinical features

GERD most commonly present as heartburn and regurgitation

heart burn is retrosternal burning sensation that may radiate to the neck that occur after meals

Regurgitation is food regurgitation into mouth or hypopharynx that occur after meals

GERD can also may present as:

Chest pain: it is hard to be differentiated from ACS

Belching

Nausea

Dental erosions: due to acid damaging teeth

Chronic cough: due to irritation of the throat

Asthma: acid act as asthma trigger

Dysphonia and hoarseness

Globus sensation

Alarm symptoms: dysphagia, odynophagia, anemia, hematemesis and weight loss

Dr. A. Dickson, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Classification

According to endoscopic and histopathologic appearance, GERD is classified into:

Non erosive reflux disease (NERD) also known as reflex esophagitis: most common type 60% of all cases

Erosive esophagitis (EE)

Barret esophagus (BE): least common

Histopathology

In all of these types, there is some histopathological changes affecting esophageal lining including inflammation, basal cell hyperplasia, papilla elongation and dilation of intercellular spaces, those are caused by gastric acid, pepsin and bile salts come into contact with esophageal lining

Erosive esophagitis is characterized by erosions and ulcer formation in the esophageal mucosa in addition to the changes above

In Barret esophagus there is also metaplastic change of the esophageal lining from stratified squamous epithelium into simple columnar epithelium in addition to the previously mentioned changes

Samir धर्म, Copyrighted free use, via Wikimedia Commons

Diagnosis

The diagnosis is made clinically (based on patient history) and response to PPI

If patient present with alarm symptoms then they are sent to be evaluated by EGD to rule out GERD complications or PUD

GERD complications: erosive esophagitis, Barret’s esophagus, esophageal stricture and esophageal adenocarcinoma

ACG guidelines recommend screening for H pylori infection in patients with GERD

Radiographic studies such as contract studies are not required for diagnosis and they are ordered only if there is suspicion of severe esophagitis, esophageal stricture, hiatal hernia and tumors

Ambulatory esophageal reflux monitoring: indicated in refractory GERD and in patients with normal endoscopy evaluation but they have GERD symptoms; it utilizes a telemetry PH capsule or a trans nasal Cath and it help in detecting acid reflex, frequency of reflux and correlation of symptoms with reflux episodes

Important Note: if there is suspicion for Acute coronary syndrome then ECG, cardiac enzymes and other tests should be done to exclude ACS because antisecretory meds might relieve pain in ACS too which make it really hard to differentiate the two diseases

Treatment

Lifestyle modifications: cornerstone of GERD therapy

Weight loss in obese patients

Avoiding meals at least 3 hours before bedtime

Maintaining good sleep hygiene as shown that minimal sleep disturbances resulted in suppression of LES relaxation => decreased acid reflux

Elevation of the head end of the whole bed by 8 inches improves GERD symptoms

Diet modification: elimination of spicy foods, carbonated beverages, caffeine, high fat foods and chocolate

Avoid bending or stooping

Medical therapy: it is indicated in patients who don’t respond to lifestyle modifications

Antacids

Antisecretory meds: H2 receptor antagonists or PPI; PPI therapy is the most effective for all types of GERD; ACG guidelines recommend PPI therapy once a day dosing before first meal of the day, if this fails then twice daily dosing is done

Prokinetic agents: e.g. metoclopramide and domperidone; prokinetic agents use in GERD is limited due to lack of data on their efficacy and also due to their profound adverse effects profile, especially their effects on CNS and CVS

Surgical therapy

Surgical therapy indications:

Patients with medically refractory GERD

Patients not compliant to lifestyle modifications or pharmacological treatment

Patients with large hiatal hernia

Patients who desire to discontinue long term pharmacological treatment

Surgical options:

Laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication

Laparoscopic anterior 180 degree fundoplication

Bariatric surgery in obese patients

Magnetic sphincter augmentation and transoral incision-less fundoplication

Complications

Erosive esophagitis: characterized by erosions or ulcers of esophageal mucosa

Esophageal strictures: chronic acid irritation of distal esophagus lead to scarring and strictures => patients present with dysphagia or food impaction ; treatment with esophageal dilation and PPI therapy

Barret esophagus: metaplastic changes; risk factors include Caucasian males older than 50, obesity, history of smoking ; with Barret esophagus there is high risk of development of esophageal adenocarcinoma

Laryngitis

Sinusitis

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

Esophageal adenocarcinoma
